ai_show_review.summary: Iconic Dark Star > Saint Stephen > The Eleven sequence shines
ai_show_review.blurb: The second set delivers a powerful Dark Star that segues into Saint Stephen and the legendary The Eleven. Jerry’s soaring guitar tone drives the jams while Phil’s bass tightens in the latter half. The acoustic first set is modest but includes a solid Uncle John’s Band.
ai_show_review.review: April 24, 1970 at Mammoth Gardens captures the Dead in a transitional moment – an acoustic opener that feels a bit sleepy before exploding into one of spring ’70’s most memorable electric stretches. After a gentle run through I Know You Rider, Monkey And The Engineer and a few early‑night classics, the band launches Easy Wind into a soaring Dark Star that flows seamlessly into Saint Stephen and then into the marathon The Eleven. Reviewers repeatedly note Jerry Garcia “going OFF” with tight, bright tone on both Dark Star and The Eleven, while Phil Lesh’s bass, initially buried in the acoustic set, comes forward to lock in during the climactic jams. A brief Bill Kreutzmann drum solo adds a percussive punctuation before the band drifts into an open‑ended jam that concludes with “It’s A Man’s World.” Though the audience recordings are muddy and suffer from drop‑outs, the performance itself remains compelling, especially for those who love the early‑70s exploratory spirit.

best_recording.reason: Most complete capture of the full set with relatively better fidelity despite mud, making the iconic Dark Star > Saint Stephen > The Eleven sequence audible.

key_highlights: Stellar Dark Star → Saint Stephen → The Eleven sequence defines the show’s high point
Jerry’s soaring guitar tone and intense soloing on The Eleven
Bill Kreutzmann’s brief drum solo adds excitement before the jam

band_performance.Jerry: Garcia delivers soaring licks and a tight, focused tone, especially on Dark Star and The Eleven where reviewers say he ‘goes OFF’ and sounds perfect.
band_performance.Phil: Lesh’s bass is hard to hear in the acoustic portion but comes forward later, providing a solid foundation for the second‑set jams.
band_performance.Bob: Weir is mostly noted for his onstage banter chant rather than instrumental contribution during this show.
band_performance.Billy: Kreutzmann contributes a brief drum solo before the jam leading into Good Lovin’ (cut), highlighting his percussive flair.
